unit.title: Contribute to and manage the change processes

summary: This unit teaches you to contribute to and manage change in a public body: understand why change is needed, use models such as Lewin and ADKAR, analyse forces, stakeholders and impact, plan and cost a change, communicate and consult, deal with resistance and protect staff wellbeing, roll out in a safe way, monitor and evaluate results, and make the change last. It is written for managers, supervisors and officers in Jamaican ministries, agencies and municipal corporations.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Public bodies change all the time: new computer systems, new laws and policies, restructuring, new buildings, new ways of serving the public. Change that is badly handled wastes money and hurts people. Change that is well handled improves service and brings staff with it.

**Change management** is the planned way of moving an organisation, a unit or a group of people from how things are done now to how they will be done. It covers the technical side (systems, procedures, buildings) and, even more, the **people side**: how people understand, feel about and adopt the change.
You may be asked to **manage** a change (as change manager or project lead) or to **contribute** to it (as a team leader, an officer or a member of a working group). This unit covers both.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, managers and officers in public bodies who will lead or take part in a change, and trainees preparing for that responsibility.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Explain why change is needed and its type
Identify drivers, use a PESTLE scan, and tell incremental from transformational change.
Apply Lewin's three stages, ADKAR and the change curve to a real situation.
Use force field analysis, stakeholder analysis, a readiness survey and an impact assessment.
Set a SMART objective, build an implementation plan, a risk register and a cost-benefit view, and set up governance.
Give early, regular, two-way communication; consult unions and staff as agreements require.
Understand why people resist, respond constructively, support wellbeing and treat staff fairly.
Choose between pilot, phased roll-out, parallel running and big bang; train staff; control scope.
Track progress, review results, record lessons and embed the change.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions on models, analysis, planning, communication, resistance and evaluation, including short sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as baseline, scope creep, change agent) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: prepare a change management plan from a case pack, and role-play a change briefing and a staff consultation meeting. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. Change projects are judged on their figures as well as on how people feel.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why change happens and the types of change

blocks.p: Change is driven by forces **outside** and **inside** the organisation. A **PESTLE** scan lists the outside drivers: **P**olitical, **E**conomic, **S**ocial, **T**echnological, **L**egal and **E**nvironmental.

head: PESTLE factor
Example in a Jamaican public body
rows: A new government priority or a national policy that all public bodies move services online
Budget cuts; the need to cut cost per transaction
Citizens expect faster service and mobile access; an ageing workforce
New software, digital payments, better broadband
New or amended law, such as data protection, procurement or employment rules
Hurricane damage, climate risk, the need to cut paper use

blocks.p: Inside drivers include poor performance, complaints, an audit finding, a new chief executive or a failing system.

The first thing staff need is **why**. When a government agency must move paper applications online within a year, as part of a national policy, the change manager should make clear first **why the change is needed and what it means for their work**.

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: Small, steady improvements to existing ways of working
A better form; a simpler step in a process
Large change to structure, culture and the way the body serves the public
Over three years, a ministry restructures and changes its whole service model
A scheduled roll-out of new software

head: Role
What the person does
rows: A senior leader, such as the head of the agency, who champions the change and secures resources
A person, inside or outside the body, who leads and helps bring about the change
Gives direction, makes key decisions and oversees progress
Respected officers from each section who share news, answer questions and pass on concerns
Affected by the change; their adoption makes it succeed

blocks.note: The sponsor's behaviour counts most. If a director tells everyone to use a new shared calendar but still books her own meetings by phone through her secretary, officers will see the change as optional and adopt it slowly.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Kurt Lewin, a psychologist, described change in three stages.

flow: Unfreeze: help people see why the present way must change
Change (or move): introduce the new way, train, support
Refreeze: make the new way the normal way, so people do not slip back

head: Stage
What the manager does
Sign it has failed
rows: Explain the case for change, show the gap between now and needed, involve people
People say 'nothing is wrong with how we do it'
Run training, support, pilot, give resources
People do not know how to use the new system
Update procedures, job descriptions, measures and rewards; remove the old way
Officers go back to paper files six months after a new tracking system started

blocks.p: ADKAR describes what each **person** needs. The letters stand for **Awareness** (of the need), **Desire** (to take part), **Knowledge** (of how), **Ability** (to do it in practice) and **Reinforcement** (to keep going). Change stalls at the first missing element.

head: Element
Question to ask
If it is missing
rows: Explain the reasons and the evidence
Do they want to take part?
Address fears; show benefits; involve them

blocks.p: If officers understand why a new case system is needed and want it to work, but nobody has shown them how to use it, **knowledge** is missing. If they have been trained but still cannot work quickly on the live system, **ability** is missing.

The **change curve** describes common emotional reactions to major change. Versions differ, but the usual pattern is: shock or denial, then anger or frustration, then a low point (worry, loss of confidence), then acceptance and exploring the new way, then commitment. People move at different speeds and may go back.

If, two weeks after a restructuring is announced, many officers are angry and complain, this is **normal**. The manager should accept it as a normal reaction, **listen and give clear facts**; arguing or punishing prolongs it.

John Kotter described eight steps for leading change, from creating urgency and building a guiding team, to creating short-term wins and anchoring the change in the culture. You do not need the full list, but note the ideas that match this unit: a clear case for change, a team that leads, a simple vision, communication, removing barriers, **quick wins** and embedding the change.

blocks.note: Use a model as a checklist, not a script. Ask which question the model raises for your situation, such as 'Have we unfrozen? Does each person have the knowledge and ability?'
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Force field analysis** lists the forces **driving** a change and those **restraining** it, and scores each (for example 1 to 5). Compare the totals, then plan to **weaken the strongest restraining forces and build support** for the driving forces.

Difference: 14 - 13 = 1. The forces are almost balanced, so the change could stall. Pushing harder on the driving side often increases resistance; it is usually better to **reduce the restraining forces** (reassure on jobs, replace equipment, give time for training).
List everyone affected and plot each group by **power** and **interest**.

head: Group
Approach
rows: Keep satisfied: brief on key points
Keep informed: listen, they often see problems

blocks.p: A **change impact assessment** finds out **who and what the change affects, and how much**: roles, skills, workload, locations, systems, customers. A **readiness survey** asks staff how ready they feel. If 56 of 160 officers say they feel ready, that is 56 / 160 = **35%**: most are not ready, and the plan needs more preparation.

Measure the starting position, the **baseline**, before the change, so that results can be compared later. Write a **SMART objective**: for example, 'Cut the average wait for a permit from 20 to 12 working days by 30 June.' A percentage change is (old - new) / old: (20 - 12) / 20 = **40% fall**.

blocks.note: Take the baseline with the same method you will use later. Otherwise you cannot show what the change achieved.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **change implementation plan** sets out the activities, timeline, resources and responsibilities for putting the change into effect.

flow: Confirm the case and the SMART objective
Set up governance: sponsor, steering committee, project lead, champions
List activities, owners, dates and milestones
Cost the change and its benefits
Build the risk register and the communication plan
Plan training and the way of rolling out
Agree how progress and results will be measured

blocks.p: A **risk register** records the possible problems of a change project, how likely and serious each is, and how each will be managed.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Response
rows: Payroll or client data moved with errors
Clean the data first; test; check totals after the move; keep the old data safe
Involve staff; train before go-live; coaching
Pilot; test; keep the old system until proven
Loss of service to the public

head: Sum
Method
Example
rows: Cost per renewal falls from J$1,200 to J$450: saving J$750 x 40,000 = J$30,000,000 a year
Project costs J$36,000,000; saves J$12,000,000 a year: 3 years
Compare percentage of work done with percentage spent
60% spent but 45% done: spending is ahead of progress, so investigate

head: Approach
What it is
Advantages
Risks
rows: Try it in one or two offices first
Finds and fixes problems before the full roll-out
Pilot site may not be typical
Roll out in stages, one office or group at a time
Spreads the workload; lessons learned as you go
Takes longer; two systems exist for a time
Old and new systems run side by side for a period
A safe fall-back; results can be compared
High risk: if it fails, it fails everywhere

blocks.p: For a large system with many offices, such as a payroll system for 13 parish offices, a **phased approach with a pilot** is usually safer than a big bang, because problems can be found and fixed with a few offices before everyone depends on it. A big bang may be justified when the old system must end on a fixed date, or when two systems cannot run together.

**Scope creep** is the uncontrolled growth of a project's aims and tasks after it starts. If senior officers keep asking for extra features, the project manager should assess each request through the **change control process**: what it adds, what it costs, how it affects time and risk, and who approves it.
**Go-live** is the date on which a new system or process first starts to be used for real work.

blocks.note: Before go-live: test the system, train the people, check the data, agree the fall-back, brief the public, and confirm who is available to help in the first week.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: People fill silence with rumours. Good communication is the manager's most powerful tool.

ul: **Early and regular**: tell people as soon as you can, then keep to a rhythm.
**Several ways**: meetings, email, notice boards, WhatsApp groups (if the body permits), one-to-ones.
**Two-way**: time for questions, and visible answers.
**Honest**: even when decisions are not made. Say what you know, what you do not know, and when you will update them.
**Consistent**: all managers give the same message.

head: Audience
What they need
Best channel
rows: Senior leaders and the steering committee
Why, what changes for me, when, what support
Early consultation on matters that affect conditions
What changes, from when, what to do
Dates and links with their work

blocks.p: Early in a change, not all decisions have been made. The most helpful message is: **'Here is what we know, what we do not know, and when we will update you.'**

When a change affects shifts, pay or conditions of staff who belong to a union, **consult the union early, as agreements require**. This is both fair and practical, since unions can help find workable solutions. Consultation means listening and being willing to change the plan; it is not a courtesy visit.

Set up ways for staff to give feedback during the roll-out (a suggestion box, a help desk, regular questions at team meetings), because **front-line staff often spot problems the plan did not foresee**. Act on feedback, and say what you have done.

blocks.note: In a change that merges offices, tell staff and the public early about location, opening hours and contacts, and give the date a long time in advance. Do not let staff learn of changes from the radio.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The most common reason is **fear of losing something they value**, such as skills, status, security, relationships or control. Other reasons: lack of information, past bad experience, too much change at once, poor timing, distrust of management, and genuine concerns that the change will not work.

head: Source of resistance
Constructive response
rows: Fear of job loss or loss of status
Give honest facts; offer training and a role in the new way
Explain why; show evidence; use trusted messengers
Training; use experienced people as trainers and champions
Phase the change; protect time for it
Be consistent and keep promises; involve union and staff representatives
Test it; if right, change the plan and say so

blocks.p: Resistance can be useful information: it may reveal problems the planners missed. **Forcing the change through with threats of discipline** is the response most likely to cause problems in the long term, because it creates hidden resistance and damages trust.

When a long-serving clerk who has run a paper filing system for 20 years criticises the new electronic system, **meet him first to hear his concerns and use his skill**. He may know the weaknesses of the old system and the points where staff will struggle.
Respected officers in each section act as **change champions**: colleagues trust them to share news and pass on concerns. Choose them for credibility, not rank.
Plan some early, visible successes, called **quick wins**, to show that the change is working and to keep people's support: for example, a first office whose queue falls in the first month.

Change can cause stress. During a restructuring, if several officers show signs of stress and worry about their future, their manager should **check in with them, share what is known and point to the support available** (the employee assistance arrangements, counselling, the human resources unit). Keep workloads reasonable, and watch for burnout.

When posts are reduced, for example from 12 supervisor posts to 8, use **clear, agreed selection criteria applied to all** and follow the employment law, the body's regulations and the agreements with unions. Be open about the process, give people time and respect, and treat those who leave with dignity. Do not make informal promises.

Where a change moves personal data (for example the records of 50,000 citizens to a new database), follow the general purpose of the data protection law: **move only the data needed, move it securely and protect it**. Check accuracy before and after the move.

blocks.note: A change that is technically perfect and ignored by staff has failed. Spend as much time on people as on systems.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Monitoring, evaluating and sustaining the change

blocks.p: Track whether the change is on course by **checking agreed measures against the plan at set points**: milestones met, budget used, training completed, user numbers, errors, complaints and staff feedback.

head: Measure
Calculation
Example
rows: 6,300 of 9,000 applications online = 70%; target 80% by year end
50% online against a 60% target: 10 percentage points short
Queue time from 40 to 25 minutes: 15 / 40 = 37.5% fall

blocks.p: A **post-implementation review** after the change **checks results against aims and records lessons**. Compare the figures with the baseline, ask staff and customers, find what worked and what did not, and decide what still needs doing.
Keep the lessons in a **shared lessons register** that future project teams can use, not in one person's notebook.

Without effort, people slip back. To make a change permanent, **build it into policies, procedures, job descriptions, work plans and performance measures**; train new staff in the new way; keep leaders using it; recognise success; and **remove the old way** (for example withdraw the paper forms) once the new way is proven.

head: Sign the change is embedded
Sign it is not
rows: Procedures and job descriptions describe the new way
Officers keep the old paper forms 'just in case'
New staff are trained in the new way as a matter of routine
Parallel running has no end date
Measures show results holding or improving
Results fall back after the project team leaves
Leaders use and talk about the new system

blocks.h: Contributing to a change when you are not the manager

blocks.p: Officers contribute in many ways: they give **evidence to the change team through the agreed channel** (for example, if an officer believes a planned change to the complaints process will make the public wait longer); join working groups; test the system; act as a champion; help colleagues; and tell the truth about problems early. A team leader asked about the effect of a proposed new shift system should give effects on **workload, service and staff, with evidence**.

blocks.note: Raise a concern with facts and in the agreed way, early: 'The test shows complaints will take two days longer because each case needs an extra approval; here are the figures.' That helps the project more than criticism in the corridor.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain why a change is needed, using PESTLE and inside drivers, and tell incremental from transformational change.
name the roles of sponsor, change manager, steering committee and change champions.
apply Lewin's unfreeze, change and refreeze, and explain what failed when staff go back to the old way.
use ADKAR to find the missing element, and the change curve to understand reactions.
carry out and score a force field analysis and say how to use the result.
analyse stakeholders by power and interest, and do an impact assessment and a readiness survey.
take a baseline and write a SMART change objective.
build an implementation plan, a risk register and a cost-benefit view.
choose between a pilot, phased roll-out, parallel running and big bang.
control scope creep through change control.
write a communication plan with early, regular, two-way messages, and consult unions as agreements require.
respond to resistance constructively, support wellbeing and treat staff fairly in a restructuring.
protect personal data during a change.
monitor progress with measures, hold a post-implementation review and keep a lessons register.
embed a change so that it lasts, and contribute positively to a change as an officer.

terms: The planned way of moving people and an organisation from the present way to the new way.
Political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental drivers of change.
Small, steady improvements to existing ways of working.
Large change to structure, culture and the way the body serves the public.
A senior leader who champions the change and secures resources.
A person who leads and helps bring about a change.
Awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement.
The common emotional reactions to major change over time.
Scoring the driving and restraining forces of a change.
The people or groups who affect, or are affected by, a change.
The figures measured before a change starts, used for later comparison.
A record of possible problems, their likelihood, seriousness and management.
A trial in a small area before wider roll-out.
Rolling out a change in stages.
Running old and new systems side by side for a period.
Uncontrolled growth of a project's aims and tasks.
The date a new system first starts to be used for real work.
A review after the change that checks results against aims and records lessons.

c1.title: Digital building permits in Portland
c1.text: The Portland Municipal Corporation will move building permit applications from paper to an online system within 12 months. The change manager, Ms Camille Henry, scores the forces. Driving: citizens want faster permits (5), national policy (4), savings on paper and storage (3), staff want less filing (2). Restraining: fear of job loss (4), old computers (4), weak internet in two outlying offices (3), little time for training (2). A readiness survey of 120 officers finds that 84 feel ready. After training, officers know how to use the system, but in the first weeks of live use they work slowly and ask for help.

c2.title: An electronic leave system for 1,200 staff
c2.text: A ministry introduces an electronic leave and attendance system for its 1,200 staff in six divisions. The project cost is J$30 million and the system is expected to save J$7.5 million a year in clerical time. Training sessions take 40 staff each. Midway through, J$18 million has been spent and the project manager, Mr Leon Campbell, judges that 45% of the work is done. Senior officers have begun asking for extra reports and links to the payroll that were not in the project's scope.

c3.title: An attendance system in a regional education office
c3.text: A regional education office is replacing paper registers of school visits with a mobile app. Mrs Hyacinth Brown, a field officer for 22 years, says openly in meetings that the app is a waste of time and that the paper system has never failed. Some younger officers are keen. The regional director has said that he will carry on using his own paper notes for his school visits. The change manager wants to plan the next steps.

c4.title: Online property fees at a parish office
c4.text: Six months ago a parish office started online payment of property fees. The aim was for 60% of the 7,800 payments in the period to be made online and for the counter queue to fall from 40 to 25 minutes. The results are that 3,900 payments were made online and the average queue is 25 minutes. Several officers still keep a handwritten ledger of payments 'just in case', and training for new staff has not been updated.

c5.title: A client database move at a social services agency
c5.text: A social services agency will move the records of 30,000 clients from a paper and spreadsheet system to a new database. A clerk, Ms Nadine Walker, who works with the files every day, thinks that the plan to switch off the old records on the go-live date will lead to missing data. The steering committee meets each month. The change manager is considering how to run the move safely.

questions.q: What are the totals of the driving and restraining forces, and what does the difference suggest?
o: 14 and 13, a difference of 1, so the forces are nearly balanced and the change may stall
14 and 13, a difference of 1, so the driving forces win and success is certain
10 and 13, a difference of 3, so the restraining forces win and the change is dropped
14 and 15, a difference of 1, so the restraining forces are stronger than the driving
questions.why: Driving: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14. Restraining: 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 13. A small difference means the change is fragile; the manager should reduce the restraining forces.

questions.q: Which approach is likely to work best on the forces Ms Henry has scored?
o: Reduce the strongest restraining forces, such as job fears and old computers, and build support
Raise the pressure on staff by announcing a firmer deadline for every office
Tackle the lowest-scoring forces first, because they are the easiest to remove
Ignore the restraining forces and tell staff only about the benefits of the change
questions.why: Pushing harder on driving forces tends to raise resistance. Weaken the strongest restraining forces (reassure on jobs, replace equipment) and build support.

questions.q: What percentage of officers feel ready, and what does the figure tell Ms Henry?
o: 70%, so three in ten are not ready and need preparation
84%, so almost all are ready and nothing more is needed
30%, so most officers are ready
70%, so no training is necessary
questions.why: 84 / 120 = 0.70 = 70%. Even a good figure leaves 36 officers who are not ready, and they need support and attention.

questions.q: Officers have been trained but work slowly on the live system. Which ADKAR element is most likely missing?
o: Ability
Awareness
Desire
Knowledge
questions.why: They know how to use it (knowledge) but cannot yet do it well in practice. Ability needs practice time, coaching and support.

questions.q: How many training sessions are needed for all 1,200 staff, and how many weeks if two sessions a week are held?
o: 30 sessions; 15 weeks
30 sessions; 30 weeks
48 sessions; 24 weeks
40 sessions; 20 weeks
questions.why: 1,200 / 40 = 30 sessions. At two sessions a week, 30 / 2 = 15 weeks.

questions.q: What is the simple payback period of the project?
o: 4 years
3 years
5 years
6 years
questions.why: J$30 million / J$7.5 million a year = 4 years. Payback is cost divided by yearly saving.

questions.q: What does the project's position, with 60% of the budget spent and 45% of the work done, suggest?
o: Spending is ahead of progress, so the cause needs investigating
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The budget is spent in step with the work, so no action is needed
The percentages cannot be compared
questions.why: 18 / 30 = 60% spent against 45% done. If the rate continues, the project will overrun its budget; find out why and take action.

questions.q: How should Mr Campbell deal with the senior officers' requests for extra reports and payroll links?
o: Assess each through change control for cost, time, risk and approval
Accept every request, since each one comes from a senior officer
Refuse all of them without looking at what each would add
Add them quietly and carry the extra cost into next year's budget
questions.why: This is scope creep. A change control process lets the sponsor or steering committee decide knowingly whether to add work, extend time or raise the budget.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason for Mrs Brown's strong criticism?
o: Fear of losing something she values, such as expertise built over 22 years
Laziness and an unwillingness to do the work she is given
A dislike of the younger officers who support the change
Not having read the project plan that was sent to her office
questions.why: The most common reason for resistance is fear of losing skills, status or control. Her long experience is also a resource the project can use.

questions.q: What should the change manager do first?
o: Meet her to hear her concerns and find a role that uses her knowledge
Warn her that discipline will follow if she keeps on criticising the change
Move her to another region without any discussion of her concerns
Leave her alone until the app is working perfectly in every office
questions.why: Listening may reveal real problems with the app, and giving an experienced officer a role (such as testing or training) turns a critic into a contributor.

questions.q: What is the likely effect of the regional director continuing to use paper notes?
o: Officers will see the change as optional and adopt it slowly
Officers will adopt the change faster, to avoid his criticism
There will be no effect, as his notes are private
The app will work better because fewer people use it
questions.why: Leaders' behaviour sets the example. If the sponsor does not use the new way, staff conclude it is not important.

questions.q: Which early success would make the best quick win for the app?
o: One district where visit records are complete and available the same day
A speech from the director about the long-term vision for the office
A memo that tells staff the old registers will be withdrawn next year
A training session held for the younger officers only
questions.why: A quick win is an early, visible result that shows the change works and builds support. Complete same-day records are something staff and managers can see for themselves.

questions.q: By how many percentage points did the office miss its online-payment target?
o: 10 percentage points
60 percentage points
780 percentage points
questions.why: 3,900 / 7,800 = 50%. The target was 60%, so the shortfall is 10 percentage points (780 payments, since 60% of 7,800 is 4,680).

questions.q: By what percentage did the average queue time fall?
Which sign shows that the new way of working is not yet embedded?
o: Officers keep a handwritten ledger in case the online system fails
The new procedure has been written into the staff handbook
Queue times have fallen and have stayed down for six months
New staff are shown the online system on their first day at work
questions.why: Keeping the old way 'just in case' shows refreezing is incomplete. Once the new way is proven, the old way should be removed.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the post-implementation review at six months?
o: Check the results against the aims and record the lessons
Decide which officers are to blame for the target that was missed
Show the funder that the project was a complete success
Start the project again from the beginning with a new plan
questions.why: A post-implementation review compares results with the aims (here, 50% against a 60% target, and the queue target met) and records lessons for future projects.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of running the old and new records systems side by side for a time?
o: To compare results and keep a safe fall-back if the new database fails
To keep staff busy for a time by giving them double entry to do
To avoid the need for any training on the new database
To save money on the cost of the new system in the first year
questions.why: Parallel running lets the agency check the new system's results against the old one and keeps a safety net, at the cost of double work.

questions.q: What is the best response to Ms Walker's concern about missing data?
o: Test the data move and check totals before switching off the old records
Tell her that the decision is made and that she should not worry about it
Switch off the old records on the go-live date, exactly as planned
Ask her to keep her concerns private until after go-live has happened
questions.why: Front-line staff often spot problems the plan did not foresee. Test the data and keep the old records until the new data is proven correct.

questions.q: Who should be able to open the new client database?
o: Only staff who need it for their work, with access recorded
All staff in the agency, so no one is held up by a missing password
Any contractor working on the move, until the move is complete
Staff and clients' relatives, to help keep the data up to date
questions.why: The data protection law's purpose is to limit the use of personal data. Access should be limited to those who need it, with a record of who looked at what.

questions.q: At the monthly steering committee, what should the change manager report?
o: Progress against milestones and budget, risks, and decisions needed
Only good news, to keep the committee supportive of the project
A list of the staff who have complained about the change
Nothing at all, because the committee only meets once a month
questions.why: A steering committee gives direction and makes key decisions, so it needs honest information on progress, risks and the decisions required.
